items.title: F-22 Pilots Awarded Distinguished Flying Cross for Actions in CENTCOM, Including Midnight Hammer
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: Seven F-22 Raptor pilots have recently been awarded one of the military’s highest decorations for their actions during operations in the Middle East. Six of the pilots were decorated with the Distinguished Flying Cross for their role in Operation Midnight Hammer, the June 2025 strikes against Iranian nuclear facilities. The post F-22 Pilots Awarded Distinguished Flying Cross for Actions in CENTCOM, Including Midnight Hammer appeared first on <a href="https://www.airands
items.body:
Seven F-22 Raptor pilots have recently been awarded one of the military’s highest decorations for their actions during operations in the Middle East.

Six of the pilots were decorated with the Distinguished Flying Cross for their role in Operation Midnight Hammer, the June 2025 strikes against Iranian nuclear facilities

Another pilot currently stationed in Europe received a DFC for a mission in the Middle East, but the Air Force did not say when or where the actions that earned that pilot the award occurred.

The six Airmen from Langley were decorated for their actions escorting B-2 Spirit stealth bombers that struck the Fordow and Natanz nuclear sites in Iran. The strike package also included F-16 Fighting Falcons and F-35 Lightning II fighters, and pilots from those units received DFCs earlier this year; tanker crews from multiple units have also received the award for supporting the mission. No individual awards have yet been announced for the B-2 aviators who participated in Midnight Hammer.

The DFC recognizes acts of heroism or extraordinary achievement in the air and is the military’s fourth-highest award for heroism.

Four of the pilots came from the Active-Duty 94th Fighter Squadron, part of the 1st Fighter Wing at Joint Base Langley-Eustis, Va., and two pilots came from the associated Virginia Air National Guard’s 149th Fighter Squadron, part of the 192nd Wing.

The medals were presented Aug. 31 by the head of Air Combat Command, Gen. Adrian L. Spain, in a ceremony at the Virginia base.

The F-22s were among an armada of fighters that escorted the seven B-2s that dropped 14 30,000-pound GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator weapons on Iran’s nuclear facilities. Around 125 U.S. aircraft of all types were involved in the mission, which came after a nearly two-week Israeli air campaign against Iran. The stealthy F-22s serve as the Air Force’s premier air-to-air fighters and can use their capabilities to penetrate defended airspace.

“Their job was to provide air superiority,” Spain said, according to an account of his remarks provided by the 1st Fighter Wing. “The bombers and the rest of the support package relied on these Raptor pilots to clear the skies, shield them from surface threats, and ensure a safe route through heavily contested airspace.”

Officials from Air Combat Command and the 1st Fighter Wing declined to provide further details on the mission that earned the pilots their decorations or medal citations, or to publicly disclose pilots’ identities, citing operational security concerns.

“We haven’t awarded many of these in the last few decades, as it’s intended to recognize true heroism and highly exceptional accomplishment in flight, which means that it should be rare, and it is,” said Spain.

Iran’s air force was largely destroyed during the 2026 air campaign against the country, Operation Epic Fury. But even during Midnight Hammer, Iran posed a limited air-to-air threat, with most of its capability consisting of aircraft purchased before the Iranian revolution in 1979. Before the Shah was overthrown and a theocratic government took over, Iran was the largest purchaser of American arms. Iran also has Soviet-designed fighters.

Still, Iran showed the ability to generate some airpower, launching aircraft to attack Gulf countries after Israel and Iran began their air campaign on Feb. 28 of this year, and was able to strike a base in Kuwait used by the U.S. with one of its aging fighter jets.

F-22s from Langley deployed to support Operation Epic Fury and follow-on actions against Iran earlier this year but have since returned.

“It was your support that enabled their excellence—from the maintainers, the operations team, the intel professionals, and the logistics involved,” Spain said. “Let there be no doubt heroism like this is earned by the entire formation. These pilots were the leading edge that day, but the foundation of their success was laid by the hard work of the entire organization in the days prior and every day since. And that’s what Air Force readiness looks like.”

The seventh F-22 pilot received their decoration Sept. 22 from U.S. Air Forces in Europe commander Lt. Gen. Jason T. Hinds for leading a strike package during a mission in the Middle East that operated in contested airspace, according to a release from the command. U.S. officials did not immediately say whether the mission was part of Operation Epic Fury, Operation Midnight Hammer, or Operation Rough Rider, the 2025 campaign against the Houthis in Yemen.

The pilot faced “challenging conditions including enemy threats” and “directed the aircraft formation, making critical decisions with limited time and little margin for error,” according to USAFE.

The command, like ACC, withheld the Airman’s identity.

“For more than an hour, [the pilot] remained focused on protecting teammates” and “acted decisively to protect the larger force, and ensured the formation could safely return,” Hinds said. “Their actions helped give the strike package the time and freedom needed to accomplish its mission.”

items.title: 94th Army Air and Missile Defense Command gets a new Deputy Commanding Officer
items.author: SFC William Tanner
items.summary: JOINT BASE PEARL HARBOR-HICKAM, Hawaii -- On Monday, September 21, 2026, the 94th Army Air and Missile Defense Command had a change at its deputy commanding officer position before their current DCO's retirement ceremony later on in the week.
items.body: JOINT BASE PEARL HARBOR-HICKAM, Hawaii -- On Monday, Sep. 21, 2026, the 94th Army Air and Missile Defense Command had a change at its deputy commanding officer position before their current DCO's retirement ceremony later on in the week. U.S. Army Col. Matthew W. Dalton relinquished the reigns to the current title of 94th AAMDC DCO to Col. Joseph C. Scott in lieu of the unit's upcoming 2026 Saint Barbara's Luau and his own retirement ceremony, both being held on Sep. 25, 2026. U.S. Army Col. Joseph C. Scott grew up an Air Force “brat,” but currently hails from Hanover, New Hampshire. He was commissioned through ROTC as an Air Defense Artillery (ADA) officer in 2000. He is married to Emily Copeland of East Walpole, Massachusetts. They have two children: Owen and Jamie. Scott’s first assignment was as a Patriot Platoon Leader and Tactical Control Officer with E Battery, 2nd Battalion, 43rd ADA at Fort Bliss, Texas and in Kuwait and Iraq during the opening months of Operation Iraqi Freedom. While at Fort Bliss, he also served as a Patriot Battalion Tactical Director (2 -43 ADA), Patriot Officer Basic Course Mentor/Instructor (3rd Battalion, 6th ADA), and Brigade Assistant S-3 (108th ADA Brigade). He then commanded B Battery, 1st Battalion, 7th ADA (Patriot) at Fort Bliss and at Osan Air Base in the Republic of Korea. Following two years of advanced civilian school, Scott served as an Instructor and Assistant Professor in the History Department at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point. He later served as the Senior Air and Missile Defense Operations Officer for XVIII Airborne Corps at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, and deployed to Afghanistan to serve as the Visitor Coordination Cell Chief for the International Security Assistance Force Joint Command (IJC) during Operation Enduring Freedom. Following redeployment, he later served in Headquarters and Headquarters Battalion, XVIII Airborne Corps, as the Battalion Operations Officer, Battalion Executive Officer, and Rear Detachment Battalion Commander. Scott then served as Deputy Commanding Officer for 31st ADA Brigade at Fort Sill, Oklahoma, and later as Commander of the 3rd Battalion, 6th ADA Regiment in the U.S. Army Air Defense Artillery School (the battalion was split between Fort Sill, Oklahoma and White Sands Missile Range, New Mexico). Following battalion command, he served as Assistant Chief of Staff, G3 (Operations) and then Chief of Staff for the 94th Army Air and Missile Defense Command (AAMDC) at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, Hawai'i. He served as Deputy Director, J8 (Requirements and Resources) for U.S. Indo-Pacific Command at Camp H.M. Smith, Hawai’i, and his most recent assignment was as Commander of the 38th ADA Brigade, headquartered at Sagami General Depot, Japan. Scott currently has a Bachelor of Arts in History from Dartmouth College, a Master of Arts in History from the University of Virginia, and a Master of Strategic Studies (Distinguished Graduate) from the U.S. Army War College. His military education includes the ADA Officer Basic Course, the ADA Captains’ Career Course, the Joint Firepower Course, Command and General Staff College, the Air Command and Staff College, and the Jumpmaster Course. His U.S. awards include the Defense Superior Service Medal, Legion of Merit, Bronze Star Medal, Parachutist Badge, and Basic Space Badge. His international awards include the NATO ISAF Medal, the Republic of Georgia’s General Kvinitadze Medal, Japan’s Defense Cooperation Award (Second Class), and German Airborne Wings (Bronze).

items.title: Air Force Adjusting Plan for Maintenance Career Overhaul from Just 7 AFSCs to 14
items.author: Matthew Cox
items.summary: The Air Force will officially kick off a major overhaul of maintenance career field next year with a pilot program, but the plan for the revamp is still evolving—while officials once intended to condense 50 aircraft maintenance specialties down to just seven, now they are targeting 14 Air Force Specialty Codes, according to Lt. Gen. Kenyon K. Bell. The post Air Force Adjusting Plan for Maintenance Career Overhaul from Just 7 AFSCs to 14 appeared first on <a href="https://www.a
items.body:
The Air Force will officially kick off a major overhaul of maintenance career field next year with a pilot program, but the plan for the revamp is still evolving—while officials once intended to condense 50 aircraft maintenance specialties down to just seven, now they are targeting 14 Air Force Specialty Codes, according to Lt. Gen. Kenyon K. Bell.

Bell, deputy chief of staff for logistics, engineering, and force protection, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a recent interview that the sweeping effort will be “a multiyear transformation” how the Air Force recruits, trains, and develops its maintenance force, suggesting it will be quite a while before that transformation is complete.

“The two-way career field strategy is on track to initiate [an 18-month] pilot test in mid- to late-2027,” said Bell, who added, “It’s going to be a yearslong effort for this to take place.”

The service first revealed its career field transformation plan for maintenance Airmen in January 2025. The strategy called for enlisted Airmen to start out on a generalist track—a single Air Force Specialty Code—where they will focus on applying the most common maintenance skills such as recovering and fueling across multiple airframes. Once Airmen reach the rank of Senior Airman and are preparing to become noncommissioned officers, they would become a specialist in one of six non-aircraft-specific areas:

- Avionics and Electrical, which combines avionics with the electrical side of the Environmental and Electrical (E&E) specialty

- Aerospace Ground Equipment, which will look the same as it does now

- Advanced Mechanical, which combines crew chiefs, fuels, hydraulics, and the flight line side of engine maintenance

- Crew Support Systems, which combines ejection seat systems with the environmental side of E&E

- Fabrication, which combines aircraft structural maintenance, aircraft metals technology, and nondestructive inspection.

- Intermediate-level engines, for maintainers dedicated to intermediate-level engine maintenance.

The New Plan

In the revised plan, the initial phase is similar. It will train maintainers entering the Air Force as aviation maintenance technicians, or AMTs, for their first 18 months of service, focusing on maintenance fundamentals for multiple airframes. The initial phase will also emphasize that the skills they are learning will ground them in the importance of aircraft sortie generation, which is a key focus of the service’s strategy to generate and sustain airpower even if under attack, Bell said.

“We’re an Air Force. We fly, fix, fight, and win. And the first thing that we want to be able to do is make sure that as all of our maintainers come in, they understand what sortie generation is about,” Bell said. “If you can’t get the aircraft off the ground, then what are we really here for?”

Maintenance Airmen will then transition into a specialty track where they will select from one of 14 different specialties, Bell said. The Air Force would not release the new specialty list because it is still refining how it will be organized, according to an Air Force spokesperson. There will be six specialties that are “aircraft-agnostic,” but it’s unclear how they will be different from the original six, the spokesperson said. Another eight specialties will be split among three different aircraft groups:

- Tactical Lift/Rotary

Air Force officials refined the plan to offer more specialties after meeting with maintenance Airmen as part of the effort’s feedback-gathering campaign that began in January.

“We stood up 10 different working groups; we brought in almost 280 different maintainers from across the Air Force to help us refine the strategy and the specifics,” Bell said. “It was long list of things that we went through.”

The revised plan offers maintenance Airmen the option to change their specialty, which is currently based on their score on the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery test that the majority of enlisted Airmen take while still in high school, Bell said.

“How well they did on that ASVAB test could probably determine what career field they went into and where they were going to spend the next 20 years of their life; something just doesn’t sit right about that,” Bell said. “And if we have the ability to now say, hey, ‘this may be where you scored and which you what you were selected for, but maybe now with a little more maturity, and now that we have shown you some other things, maybe there’s a different path still within the aircraft maintenance career field … maybe you want to choose this specialty over another.’ So, I’m really excited about that aspect of it. There is a little more optionality that also matches up with Air Force needs.”

Eventually, maintainers in the specialty track will have the opportunity to apply for the master aviation technician, or MAT, track—a more specialized pipeline designed to create a smaller force of highly skilled maintainers who will focus on fixing more complex problems on specific aircraft, Bell said.

But the highly selective pipeline is only designed for a “small percentage of maintenance force; that’s going to cultivate them into cross-functional technical experts on a specific aircraft.”

“That small percentage of folks will help us ensure that as people move around, that MAT group of folks will be that core group of folks that we lean on to be those very technical experts to solve some of the hard breaks, the hard problems that might go on the aircraft,” Bell said.

When it was first revealed, the new strategy sparked concerns among current and former Air Force maintainers that the new design could dilute expertise across the career field and reduce local leaders’ ability to solve complex maintenance problems.

“I’m not going to say that that is not a valid concern, but with any change, you’re going to have some amount of pushback to it,” Bell said, adding that that is why the service sought feedback from current maintainers.

“I take all input, and that’s the reason why we have asked the major commands to send me your brightest people who can represent you, who are going to be constructive disruptors,” Bell said.

“To the maintenance Airmen that said, ‘I’m a naysayer and I don’t believe you in this’: give me your input and then help us try to mitigate that,” Bell added. “We can’t continue to do what we’re doing now and think that we’re going to get a different result.”

Critics also question how the Air Force would switch to the new model amid a shortage in maintenance manning.

Bell said that a key benefit of the 2A career field transformation is it will instill in young maintainers the importance of aircraft sortie generation similar to the way Air Force is stressing “airmindedness” in Basic Military Training and tech school to ensure Airmen understand they have a role in generating combat airpower.

“This particular line of effort that we’re doing right now with the two-way career field strategy speaks to retention because we believe that as more maintainers come in and then we train them up in this way, this ability to be sortie generators up front is going to add to their motivation and their reason for being,” Bell said.

“People want to add value, and their ability to be sortie generators early will show that they can add value—that’s why this two-way career field strategy, I believe, is going to be a benefit for us in the retention area.”

items.title: PMTEC, USARPAC Share Innovation Insights at AFCEA Hawaii Luncheon
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: Personnel from the U.S. Pacific Command (US PACOM) J7 Pacific Multi-Domain Training and Experimentation Capability (PMTEC) and U.S. Army Pacific (USARPAC) shared perspectives on artificial intelligence, space as a contested domain, information operations and rapid experimentation with government and industry partners during the Armed Forces Communications and Electronics Association (AFCEA)-Hawaii Luncheon Series on Sept. 8, 2026.
items.body:
JOINT BASE PEARL HARBOR-HICKAM, Hawaii — Personnel from the U.S. Pacific Command (US PACOM) J7 Pacific Multi-Domain Training and Experimentation Capability (PMTEC) and U.S. Army Pacific (USARPAC) shared perspectives on artificial intelligence, space as a contested domain, information operations and rapid experimentation with government and industry partners during the Armed Forces Communications and Electronics Association (AFCEA)-Hawaii Luncheon Series on Sept. 8, 2026. The panel, moderated by Brent Parker, PMTEC industry engagement lead, featured Dr. Andre Stridiron, PMTEC program manager; Andy Emslie, PMTEC space integrator; Tai Prohaska, PMTEC information integrator; and Col. Jeremy Schunke, USARPAC director of concepts. Their insights illustrated how PMTEC’s experimentation pipeline, information integration, and space-domain initiatives contribute to modernization, building a more agile, lethal, and resilient force.

AI Transforming Training and Rehearsal Stridiron opened the discussion, by describing how PMTEC integrated AI during exercise Valiant Shield 26 to replicate opposing forces at a scale and speed far beyond the capacity of human operators. “In the past, one person could maybe replicate two or three entities in a synthetic environment,” Stridiron said. “In Valiant Shield 26, we were able to bring in AI tools that are informed by intel and can not only react and respond at scale and at scope, but also in real time to the blue force reactions. “What that’s doing is increasing the fidelity of training, increasing the scope and scale, and the realism of what our warfighters are now preparing for.”

Stridiron emphasized the need to train the entire kill chain — find, fix, track, target, engage and assess — rather than focusing only on the kinetic “boom” phase, and stressed interoperability across joint and coalition tools. “AI is only as good as the data,” Stridiron said. “We have to have humans in the loop.” That human factor includes trust.

“Security of high-end AI tools used for intelligence and decision-making remains a work in progress that exercises help illuminate,” Stridiron said.

Space as a Contested, Enabling Domain Emslie outlined how US PACOM leverages space capabilities for situational awareness and deterrence as U.S. Space Forces Pacific (SPACEPAC) grew from about 25 personnel in 2022 to approximately 150 today. According to Emslie, J7 funded, PMTEC operations, activities and investments (OAIs) are creating realistic training environments that integrate space into joint force planning and execution.

Those OAIs include the WestPac Space Range, which will allow forces to practice communications under simulated jamming and enable space electronic warfare against simulated adversary satellite signals — without risking real-world assets. Additional investments include automated targets equipped with emitters that can appear as various surface craft in the live-virtual-constructive environment, allowing joint and coalition forces to execute the full kill chain against electromagnetic threats before kinetic operations. Emslie said investments also include hiring personnel to strengthen exercise planning and commercial-military space integration.

“It’s a really exciting time to be part of the space community,” Emslie said. “It’s also very fertile ground for anybody that wants to get involved in helping build the space community, train space warfighters and sharpening Guardians as we move forward.”

Operating in the Information Environment Stating that the information environment is a warfighting domain, Prohaska emphasized the importance of controlling the narrative to impact knowledge, attitudes and behaviors. She cited historical and contemporary examples — from Vietnam War-era media embedding to Ukraine’s current sovereignty narrative — to illustrate how public and global opinion influence decision-making and warfighting outcomes.

“PMTEC’s very existence is a deterrence, but only if people know about it,” Prohaska said. “We are making a concentrated effort to amplify the success stories that we’re having with our allies and partners, with our industry partners, with our warfighters who are often the early adopters of technology.”

According to Prohaska, PMTEC is investing in telling stories that support themes and messages that ultimately contribute to credible deterrence. PMTEC’s information integration includes working with planners and public affairs personnel to ensure the information space is considered during exercise planning. During exercise execution, PMTEC supports U.S., ally and partner public affairs through the Combined Joint Information Bureaus, providing strategic guidance, content and access to subject matter experts to explain advanced technology, demonstrated capabilities and their strategic impacts. Many of these innovations are achieved alongside allies and partners.

“When we are training bilaterally or multi-laterally, we want to make sure that we are all on the same page, so that we speak with a unified voice,” Prohaska said. “That demonstrates interoperability with our allies and partners, which is one of our biggest asymmetric advantages.”

Forward Experimentation and Operational Capability Innovation Schunke described a campaign level process, PIPELINE, that begins with key operational problems drawn from the threat, emerging technology or commander guidance, moves through future-oriented war games, requirements roundups, and then into experimentation. PMTEC funding enables the critical middle step of testing solutions against real operational gaps.

Recent successes include the Battlefield Assisted Trauma Distributed Observation Kit–Joint (BATDOK-J), which captures tactical combat casualty care data at the point of injury, routes it through successive echelons of care, and populates permanent medical records. Iterative PMTEC-supported experimentation culminated during exercise Balikatan 26 and is now on a path to program-of-record status for joint medical operations. “Experiment needs to be one of three things,” Schunke said. “[One,] success, we scale. [Two,] if there can be a tweak to it, we modify, or … [three], we stop and we don’t continue. Those are those hard decisions that we have to make.”

Schunke said the culture of innovation already exists among Soldiers, industry and academia; the challenge is the “connective tissue” — clearly communicating operational problems rather than developing shopping lists.

Aligning with Department Innovation Transformation The panel’s themes advanced the Secretary of War’s January 2026 memorandum, “Transforming the Defense Innovation Ecosystem to Accelerate Warfighting Advantage.” That directive organizes efforts around three outcomes — technology innovation, product innovation and operational capability innovation — and demands delivery at the speed of relevance with clear accountability.

According to the panel, PMTEC operationalizes the third outcome — operational capability innovation — by combining technologies, tactics and doctrine into new ways of fighting at the forward edge. Its live-virtual-constructive architecture, AI-enabled opposing forces, space range investments, information-domain amplification and service-linked demonstrations equip portfolio acquisition executives and program offices with the last-mile insertion pathways.

Industry engagement through problem-driven and product-driven channels, term-limited talent rotation principles, and rigorous go/modify/stop decisions mirror the memo’s emphasis on mission command, measurable outcomes and termination of efforts that no longer justify perseverance. Industry leaders attending the event acknowledged PMTEC’s role in bridging commercial technological advancement directly to the operational force.

“PMTEC is paramount — it is the glue between industry and the military services out here,” said Maurice Anstead, business development director for Peraton. “It provides a clear path for industry to bring the best of capability and get that into the experimentation cycle. In the past, the question was: How do we get these great capabilities into the hands of the warfighter? PMTEC is that mechanism to bring innovative ideas to the warfighter today.”

About PMTEC Established in 2022, the Pacific Multi-Domain Training and Experimentation Capability is a U.S. Pacific Command, J7enterprise that integrates live, virtual and constructive training technologies into a unified, scalable and persistent ecosystem. It links geographically dispersed ranges, resources and warfighters, enabling U.S. and allied forces to rehearse complex mission sets in realistic, threat-informed environments. PMTEC is a cornerstone of the Pacific Deterrence Initiative and directly supports National Defense Strategy priorities to defend the homeland, deter aggression and empower allies and partners.

items.title: Better Sleep, Better Readiness: Naval Health Research Center Leads Charge for Evaluating New Shipboard Mattresses
items.author: Danielle Cazarez
items.summary: Naval Health Research Center (NHRC) launched the latest phase of its ongoing effort to ensure sailor rest and warfighter readiness by evaluating the next-generation mattresses on guided-missile destroyer USS Paul Hamilton (DDG 60).
items.body: SAN DIEGO - Naval Health Research Center (NHRC) launched the latest phase of its ongoing effort to ensure sailor rest and warfighter readiness by evaluating the next-generation mattresses on guided-missile destroyer USS Paul Hamilton (DDG 60). This latest milestone, building on years of fleet surveys, laboratory testing and smaller-scale shipboard evaluations of different mattress types, moves the research from prototype testing to an operational evaluation supporting mattress modernization across U.S. Naval Surface Forces. This research is a direct response to feedback from Sailors and recommendations from the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO). Additionally, NHRC took into account recommendations from the U.S. Naval Surface Forces’ Afloat Surface Climate Assessment Survey, which identified sleep and fatigue as critical factors impacting Navy readiness. NHRC researchers diagnosed root causes of poor rest and fatigue, including identifying uncomfortable shipboard mattresses as a primary barrier to restorative rest while Sailors are underway. In the most recent stage of this study, sleep physiology researchers outfitted each berthing rack aboard the Paul Hamilton with newly engineered foam mattresses. NHRC had previously led evaluation of these mattresses for use by Sailors. NHRC's sleep researchers have conducted multiple phases of testing and surveys with support from the Office of Naval Research (ONR). The work began with upgrading NHRC’s sleep laboratory in 2024 to include a high-fidelity simulated shipboard berthing compartment. An initial laboratory pilot study showed that a commercial soft foam mattress was subjectively superior to the standard-issue Navy innerspring mattress. A larger, more comprehensive study aboard Whidbey Island-class dock landing ship USS Germantown (LSD 42) was conducted in April 2025. This study found that a softer foam mattress performed better across nearly all subjective measures, including comfort, sleep quality and feeling rested upon awakening. In parallel, a novel mattress-focused survey conducted by NHRC, which has gathered responses from almost 900 sailors, showed most sailors rating their sleep quality as poor, and stating that the mattresses increase their fatigue levels. "These Sailor-informed ratings and design preferences are intended to guide ongoing efforts to develop and test next-generation shipboard mattresses," said Evan Chinoy, NHRC’s principal investigator for the mattress study. "Sailors gave us clear, unambiguous guidance on what they need: sleeping surfaces that are softer, provide ergonomic support, and better regulate body temperature within compact berthing spaces." The data gathered by NHRC informed ONR Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) research efforts to develop new shipboard mattress designs with small business partners. Through their contracts with ONR, the small businesses and their university partners are researching and engineering custom prototype mattresses designed to meet stringent shipboard material and safety specifications, while aiming to improve mattresses to better deliver rest and fatigue recovery. In late 2025, the NHRC sleep research team tested the first batch of prototype mattresses with over 100 sailors aboard the amphibious assault ship USS Essex (LHD 2), yielding positive evaluations. Following the initial Essex study, the Navy began a limited rollout of the new mattresses to several Surface Forces ships, with NHRC leading the study to assess the performance of these mattresses over time. The mattress installation and study launch on the Paul Hamilton will mark NHRC’s most comprehensive mattress evaluation to date. With the replacement of berthing mattresses across the entire ship, NHRC researchers can assess the real-world impacts on rest, recovery and readiness. NHRC, part of Navy Medicine Research & Development, supports Navy, Marine Corps and joint U.S. warfighter health readiness and lethality with research and development that delivers high-value, high-impact solutions to the health and readiness challenges that the U.S. military population faces on the battlefield, at-sea, home and abroad.

items.title: Camp Pendleton Hosts 84th Annual Evening Colors Ceremony
items.author: Sgt Haley Fourmet Gustavsen

items.title: US Navy awards RTX’s Raytheon $24.4B for SM-6 missiles amid stockpile concerns
items.author: Mike Stone, Reuters
items.summary: The deal for the SM-6 interceptors comes as the Pentagon pushes to replenish munitions stockpiles depleted by conflicts in the Middle East.
items.body:
RTX’s Raytheon unit won a multiyear contract worth up to $24.4 billion to produce Standard Missile-6 interceptors for the U.S. Navy, the service said on Thursday, as the Pentagon pushes to replenish munitions stockpiles depleted by conflicts in the Middle East.

The five-year contract, which includes two additional option years, the Navy said, is meant to provide a steady and reliable supply of the SM-6, a missile that can carry out both offensive strikes and missile defense missions.

The SM-6 award is the latest in a series of large munitions contracts the Pentagon has pursued this year to pressure contractors into ramping up output. It follows a $20.7 billion provisional multiyear deal for Raytheon’s AMRAAM air-to-air missiles in late September and a $58.6 billion Patriot interceptor deal awarded to Lockheed Martin in July.

The production agreements are designed to entice contractors to move faster while surging production. They are part of a broader push by the Trump administration to prioritize weapons production over shareholder returns.

Industry executives have warned that Congress has not yet appropriated funding for the deals, meaning contractors may be unable to invest at scale in components and facilities until lawmakers act.

RTX has said it has invested heavily to keep up with rising demand. It has expanded its skilled workforce, strengthened partnerships across the defense industrial base and automated production, with the aim of significantly increasing output for near- and long-term needs.

Raytheon says the SM-6 is the only combat-proven weapon that can perform anti-air warfare, anti-surface warfare and ballistic missile defense. It has been fired from a range of Navy ships as well as from land-based launchers.

items.title: 1st Cavalry Division Troopers set the standard with paramedic training
items.author: SGT Jesse Rugg
items.summary: Six Troopers from the 1st Cavalry Division graduated from the Initial Paramedic Education Course at Central Texas College, marking a milestone in advanced combat trauma care for the Fort Hood military base. Over nine months, the Soldiers balanced rigorous coursework with demanding field practice alongside civilian first responders. “This was the first group of Soldiers from the 1st Cavalry Division to complete the program,” said Sgt. Maj. Waylon Wren, 1st Cavalry Division’s Chief Medical NCO. “P
items.body:
KILLEEN, Texas — Six Troopers from the 1st Cavalry Division graduated from the Initial Paramedic Education Course at Central Texas College, marking a milestone in advanced combat trauma care for the Fort Hood military base.

Over nine months, the Troopers balanced rigorous coursework with demanding field practice alongside civilian first responders.

“This was the first group of Troopers from the 1st Cavalry Division to complete the program,” said Sgt. Maj. Waylon Wren, 1st Cavalry Division’s Chief Medical NCO. “Paramedic certification provides a nationally recognized credential and strengthens professional development and preparation for advanced clinical, instructional, and operational opportunities.”

While standard Army combat medics are certified at the basic Emergency Medical Technician level, this pilot initiative bridges the gap between basic field triage and advanced trauma medicine.

“Cumulatively, the program is a thousand hours of didactic mixed with Emergency Medical Services,” said Spc. David Hernandez, a combat medic assigned to the 3rd Cavalry Regiment. “You have the classroom portion on Tuesdays learning different pathologies and illnesses, and then on Thursdays you practice assessments and hands-on skills.”

The program's true test came during real-world clinical rotations, when students stepped out of simulated environments and into emergency rooms and civilian ambulances.

“When you actually do an EMS ride-out or work in the emergency room is when you get to put it into practice,” Hernandez said. “You start IVs, you intubate, and I even got to do a finger thoracotomy — cutting into the chest wall to decompress it when a patient has blood in their lungs.”

Those hours in local hospitals required the Troopers to integrate directly into healthcare teams, treating civilian patients across various departments.

“Out in the populace, you had to do field experience in different areas of medicine,” said Staff Sgt. Brian Hoskins, a combat medic assigned to the 2nd Battalion, 8th Cavalry Regiment. “EMS was the biggest one, along with the emergency room. In the ER setting, we acted essentially as nurse assistants, performing anything within our medical scope of practice.”

For Hoskins, that level of exposure highlighted the need for higher baseline standards across the force.

“I hope this goes widespread throughout the Army,” Hoskins said. “To effectively lead, you need knowledge.” He added that the program provides that knowledge and will improve the future of Army medicine. Hernandez echoed that sentiment, emphasizing that advanced medical authority should become standard for unit leaders rather than an exception.

“This isn’t a program that should be gatekept,” Hernandez said. “If you are a 68W noncommissioned officer, being a paramedic should be the baseline requirement. In EMS, you can’t lead a medical team to its fullest capability as an EMT-B. You have to expand your skill set.”

Beyond elevating unit readiness, the certification significantly enhances the Troopers’ personal and professional trajectory, both in uniform and as potential civilian job seekers.

“Outside of the physician assistants and doctors, we are now the highest level of medically educated personnel in our units,” Hoskins said. “That knowledge will drive excellence across our peers and subordinates. And if you transition out of the military, leaving with a paramedic certification is far superior to leaving as a basic EMT.”

Ultimately, the high-pressure environment of real emergency care provided a level of psychological stress inoculation that classroom simulations simply cannot replicate.

“It teaches you resilience and how to remain calm under pressure, especially with a critical patient,” Hernandez said. “You can't lose control. You have to regulate your emotions and stay focused on what the next step is for the patient to make it to the hospital.”

He emphasized that the stress isn't something you can simulate. You have to experience the stakes, because real pressure forces you to better yourself.

“Paramedic-qualified Troopers bring stronger assessment, resuscitation, and patient-management skills to their formation,” said Wren. “They also serve as prehospital care subject-matter experts who coach other medics and improve casualty response training, evacuation rehearsals, and care during delayed evacuation.”

Graduates of the course are eligible to apply to take the test for the National Registry paramedic certification, a credential recognized across civilian emergency medical systems.

items.title: A New Adventure, A Larger Purpose: Long Joins Navy Nurse Corps
items.author: CPO Coryann Pittman
items.summary: After more than a decade of caring for others as a nurse, Nikki Long began a new chapter of service Sept. 28, 2026, when she was commissioned as a Lieutenant Junior Grade in the U.S. Navy Nurse Corps.
items.body: ST. LOUIS — After more than a decade of caring for others as a nurse, Nikki Long began a new chapter of service Sept. 28, 2026, when she was commissioned as a Lieutenant Junior Grade in the U.S. Navy Nurse Corps. Long’s commissioning ceremony was held on the quarterdeck of Headquarters, Navy Talent Acquisition Group Mid America, where Col. Fulton, U.S. Air Force, administered the oath of office. Surrounded by family, Long officially began her journey as a Navy Nurse Corps officer, bringing more than 10 years of nursing experience and a commitment to serving others with her into the Navy. “The foundation of nursing is service to others,” said Long. “I was looking for something new, and what better way to continue that service to others than to join the Navy Nurse Corps?” Long’s connection to military service began long before she took the oath herself. Her father served in the U.S. Air Force, and she said she has always admired her husband Charles’ military service. Charles, also an Air Force veteran, was among the family members present to witness her commissioning, along with their son Chayse and daughters Charlie and August. Although Long’s older son, Charles Jr., and daughter Arianna were unable to attend the ceremony in person, both remained an important part of the milestone. Arianna is also serving in the U.S. Navy, adding another chapter of military service to the Long family. For Long, joining the Navy Nurse Corps offered an opportunity to combine her nursing career with a desire to serve in a larger capacity. “I’m interested in the Navy’s humanitarian missions,” said Long. “I wanted to start this new adventure with something that’s bigger than myself while continuing to serve others.” Long’s nursing experience provides her with a strong foundation as she transitions into military service. Her decision to join the Navy Nurse Corps allows her to continue a career centered on caring for others while contributing to the Navy’s mission and supporting Sailors, Marines and their families. Her commissioning represents more than the beginning of a new professional chapter. It is also a continuation of a family tradition of service from her father and husbands Air Force service to her daughter’s service in the Navy, and now her own commitment to serve as a Navy Nurse Corps officer. With a career already centered on caring for others, Long now begins a new chapter of service, one she hopes will allow her to make an impact beyond herself while continuing to serve others through the Navy.

items.title: Marines Achieve FY26 Recruiting Mission, Secure Strong Start for FY27
items.author: Jim Edwards
items.summary: MARINE CORPS BASE QUANTICO, VA. —Marine Corps Recruiting Command (MCRC) exceeded its Fiscal Year 2026 recruiting mission across every component and category, leading a historic, department-wide rebound in military enlistments.
items.body:
MARINE CORPS BASE QUANTICO, VA. —Marine Corps Recruiting Command (MCRC) exceeded its Fiscal Year 2026 recruiting mission across every component and category, leading a historic, department-wide rebound in military enlistments.

Defying national trends and proving that the appeal of elite service remains unmatched, the Marine Corps' relentless recruiting force accessed 31,250 Enlisted Marines, 1,672 Officers, and 3,503 Prior Service Reserve Marines in FY26. Notably, Marine Recruiters maintained the Corps' legendary high-quality standards, exceeding Department of War (DoW) accession baselines in all categories.

This achievement directly aligns with the War Department’s emphasis on the “Value of Service.”

"Our success this year is a testament to the disciplined execution of our elite recruiting force on the streets of America," said Maj. Gen. Walker M. Field, Commanding General, MCRC. "Likewise, it is emblematic of the legion of young Americans who are choosing, of their own volition, to serve this great Nation of ours. The few young Americans who earn the title of Marine espouse the rare trifecta of physical, intellectual, and moral fortitude to become elite warriors."

While recruiting duty remains challenging, the landscape in FY26, to include honoring the Nation’s 250th birthday, was the most favorable the Marine Corps has operated in the past five years. Driven by a high volume of interested applicants and paired with historically strong retention rates across the Corps, Marine recruiters did not just meet their goals, they aggressively postured the Corps for the future. Remarkably, MCRC has already contracted more than half of its entire FY27 mission, establishing a resilient, ready start pool.

"Our Marines have performed superbly, and they represent our Corps with pride and honor," said Sgt. Maj. Jesse J. Dorsey, the MCRC Sergeant Major.

This sustained success is directly aligned with and accelerated by what Secretary of the Navy calls the Department’s “fight for the narrative,” a unified public messaging strategy that ensures the American people understand the unmatched career, educational, and professional value of military service.

For more information on the elite path to becoming a Marine, visit http://www.Marines.com or contact 1-800-MARINES.

items.title: Unclaimed heroes reach final resting place at KVCC
items.author: Savannah Baird
items.summary: For a total of 313 years, four months and 12 days their remains were unclaimed. They were Soldiers, Sailors, Marines and Airmen who served during pivotal war-time periods. On Sept. 30, nine service members and one military spouse were finally laid to rest during a ceremony at Kentucky Veterans Cemetery Central, claimed by more than 100 members of the greater Fort Knox community.
items.body:
Radcliff, Ky. — For a total of 313 years, four months and 12 days their remains were unclaimed.

They were Soldiers, Sailors, Marines and Airmen who served during pivotal war-time periods.

On Sept. 30, nine service members and one military spouse were finally laid to rest during a ceremony at Kentucky Veterans Cemetery Central, claimed by more than 100 members of the greater Fort Knox community.

Cpl. Eugene Morris McGlasson, U.S. Army, World War II – unclaimed for six years, four months and 26 days

Tech. 4th grade John C. Siewertsen, U.S. Army, World War II – unclaimed for 43 years, five months and 14 days

Pvt. George Sivak, U.S. Army, World War II – unclaimed for 28 years, 10 months and 20 days

Seaman Aubrey Vaughn, U.S. Navy, Korean War – unclaimed for 34 years, one month and 12 days

Seaman First Class Joseph W. Grinstead, U.S. Navy, World War II era – unclaimed for 29 years, 8 months and two days

Cpl. Steven Wayne Sturtivan, U.S. Marine Corps, post-Vietnam era – unclaimed for 37 years, 4 months and one day

Pvt. Donnie Pulliam, U.S. Marine Corps, Korean War – unclaimed for 27 years, 4 months and 23 days

Army Pvt. and Air Force Staff Sgt. William Jefferson Cardwell, U.S. Army and U.S. Air Force, World War II and Korean War – unclaimed for 44 years, 5 months and one day

Staff Sgt. Willis S. Vaughan, U.S. Air Force, World War II and Korean War – unclaimed for 30 years, 8 months and 9 days

Elsie G. Vaughan, military spouse of Staff Sgt. Willis S. Vaughan – unclaimed for 31 years, 5 months and 26 days

For each branch of service a flag was folded with precision, for each name a brass bell solemnly tolled.

“The word "unclaimed" describes what happened to their remains. It does not describe their worth,” said Chaplain (Capt.) Virgil Pop, V Corps. “We may have never met them, but gratitude does not require personal acquaintance. Today, our presence becomes our testimony.”

A testimony, he said, to honor and remembrance.

Frederick Behnke, https://www.miap.us/ Kentucky state coordinator, said the remains were all received from Arch L. Heady Funeral Homes in Louisville after research identified them as honorable service members and a dependent. Exemplifying the Missing in America Project motto, “It’s the right thing to do,” Behnke said he and his wife worked diligently to bring these heroes to a peaceful resting place.

“Every time we inter those that have been unclaimed for years, it's very, very special – it’s owed to them,” said Behnke. “They don't join the service to get anything out of the government. All they asked for was, ‘When I'm gone, give me an honorable military funeral’.

“When we find them, they're like family to us. It's up to all of us to become their family and not let them be forgotten.”

Col. David Holstead, Fort Knox garrison commander, stood among the service members attending the ceremony. For him, the day was a reminder of a purpose that connects all members of the Armed Forces – past and present.

“For those of us currently serving in uniform, it is incredibly important that we pay homage and tribute to those that came before us,” he said “This is especially true for those who answered nations’ call during times of war, as many of these heroes did.

“To be there, recognizing these veterans after all these years was truly an honor. There’s nowhere else I would rather be.”

As the final ring of the 21-gun salute sounded, attendees turned to face those being honored as the sound of taps bellowed around them.

Henderson County JROTC cadets then carried them to their final resting places.

“The flag can honor them, taps can mourn them, the earth can receive them, but only God can answer them at the grave,” said Pop. “They were known by name. They were remembered with gratitude. They were laid to rest with honor, and may they rest in peace.”

*Visit Fort Knox News at www.army.mil/knox for all of Central Kentucky's latest military news and information.*

items.title: Hawaiʻi National Guard Provides Power to Kauaʻi Humane Society After Hurricane Lowell
items.author: Rachel Blaire
items.summary: The Hawaiʻi National Guard provided emergency backup power to the Kauaʻi Humane Society following Hurricane Lowell after the organization’s existing generator became inoperable, ensuring the facility could continue essential animal-care operations during the island’s recovery.
items.body:
The Hawaiʻi National Guard provided emergency backup power to the Kauaʻi Humane Society following Hurricane Lowell after the organization’s existing generator became inoperable, ensuring the facility could continue essential animal-care operations during the island’s recovery.

Hurricane Lowell brought heavy rainfall, strong winds and hazardous conditions to Kauaʻi, contributing to road damage, disruptions to essential services and impacts to communities across the island.

“After losing utility power, our generator failed 48 hours after Hurricane Lowell made landfall,” said Allegra Kanna Scribner from Marketing & Communications of the Kauaʻi Humane Society. “Without power, our in-shelter operations were extremely limited. More alarmingly, our refrigerated vaccines were becoming compromised and our power-reliant water well stopped working, meaning our animals would soon completely run out of water.”

Hawaiʻi National Guard personnel on Kauaʻi conducted a feasibility assessment and coordinated with the Kauaʻi Emergency Management Agency and local utility personnel to determine the requirements for connecting and operating a generator at the facility.

The assessment determined that a 60-kilowatt Hawaiʻi National Guard diesel generator could meet the Humane Society’s requirements. Hawaiʻi National Guard personnel were then sourced to support the mission, while coordination with the Kauaʻi County Department of Public Works was established to transport the generator to the facility.

Staff Sgt. Kamakanilawaialii Pickering-Stevens, Power Pro Shop, 154th Civil Engineering Squadron, Hawaiʻi Air National Guard, was among the airmen supporting the mission.

“Today we're providing power to the Kauaʻi Humane Society, supporting them in their operations,” said Pickering-Stevens. “It feels great to come out here and help serve the community, helping these guys in these challenging times, just giving them peace of mind that they have the power that they need.”

The generator was connected and operational on Sept. 15, restoring full power to the shelter and allowing the Humane Society to resume its normal operations.

“This generator restored full power to our shelter, allowing us to operate at full capacity, continue caring for over 400 animals in our building, and support our community through operations like our twice-weekly Community Care Center,” said Scribner.

The mission also provided the Humane Society with additional resilience after utility power was restored. The Hawaiʻi National Guard generator remained available as a backup while the organization worked to repair its primary generator.

“Even after utility power was restored, the Hawaiʻi National Guard continued to provide a back-up generator support so our veterinarian team could safely and successfully proceed with animal surgeries with confidence,” said Scribner.

With repairs to the Humane Society’s primary generator completed, on Sept. 29, Hawaiʻi National Guard personnel disconnected and removed the generator.

“As we continue to recover from Hurricane Lowell, we are extremely grateful for all of the support we have received from the men and women of the Hawaiʻi National Guard, and for their presence and hard work during our time of need,” said Scribner.

The generator mission is one of several Hawaiʻi National Guard efforts supporting Kauaʻi following Hurricane Lowell. Hawaiʻi National Guard soldiers and airmen have worked alongside county and community partners on food distribution, traffic control, debris removal, transportation and other recovery missions.

items.title: Ukraine deploys FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for first time, Zelenskyy says
items.author: Reuters
items.summary: Ukraine has deployed its FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday.
items.body:
Ukraine has deployed its FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday.

“Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile FP-7. First combat use,” Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram. “Thank you for the result. Next - production.”

He did not say where the FP-7 had been used in combat or against what target.

Russia frequently uses ballistic missiles in strikes on Ukrainian targets, and Ukraine has viewed development of its own tactical ballistic missiles as an important element in ensuring its defense needs.

Zelenskyy praised the test results of tactical ballistic missiles earlier this year, saying they showed good potential for their use by the military.

Ukrainian military analysts describe the FP-7 as a short-range missile with a range of about 200 km (125 miles).

The missile’s manufacturer, Fire Point, says it is being developed as a ballistic interceptor within the European missile defense programme Freyja launched this year.

Ukraine wants a prototype for the Freyja European anti-ballistic system to be ready in the first half of next year, Davyd Aloian, deputy secretary of Ukraine’s National Security and Defence Council said in July.

items.title: Fort Buchanan highlights lithium battery safety during Fire Prevention Week
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: Installation leaders and firefighters gathered at command headquarters Sept. 30 to mark Fire Prevention Week, raise awareness of lithium-ion battery hazards and promote safe charging, storage and handling practices across the community.
items.body:
FORT BUCHANAN, Puerto Rico — Installation leaders and firefighters gathered at command headquarters Sept. 30 to mark Fire Prevention Week, raise awareness of lithium-ion battery hazards and promote safe charging, storage and handling practices across the community.

This year’s theme, “Charge into Fire Safety: Safe Charging is a Superpower,” focuses on batteries commonly used in cellphones, laptops, scooters, power tools and other electronic devices.

Fernando J. Vélez, assistant fire chief of prevention at Fort Buchanan Fire and Emergency Services, said lithium batteries are the campaign’s primary safety focus this year.

“This year, the big focus is lithium batteries — scooters, phones and everything running off them,” Vélez said. “Year-round, we’re doing nonstop inspections, but this is where we’re going to be focusing our message and teaching people about safety.”

During the event, Acting Garrison Manager Ulises Marrero signed a proclamation supporting the campaign and encouraging the community to make fire safety part of daily life.

“As important as it is to put out fires, as you do all the time, I think it’s more important to prevent those fires,” Marrero said. “You do a tremendous job.”

Damaged batteries, excessive heat, improper storage and the use of incorrect charging equipment can increase the risk of fire. Firefighters encourage community members to follow manufacturer instructions, use approved chargers and inspect batteries and devices for signs of damage.

Fire Prevention Week gives the department an opportunity to highlight a specific safety concern while reinforcing its year-round mission of identifying hazards and educating the community.

Fort Buchanan Fire and Emergency Services also conducts outreach with local schools and community organizations, extending its fire safety message beyond the installation.

Community members seeking additional information about lithium-ion battery safety or fire prevention may contact Fort Buchanan Fire and Emergency Services at 787-707-3410.

Fort Buchanan supports approximately 15,000 military personnel, including active-duty Soldiers, Army Reserve, Puerto Rico National Guard, Marine Corps Reserve and Navy Reserve members. The installation’s mission is to enable readiness and facilitate the deployment of forces anytime, anywhere.

items.title: JBM-HH Hosts Inaugural Legacy Leaders Forum
items.author: Jason Shepherd
items.summary: Joint Base Myer-Henderson Hall hosted its inaugural Legacy Leaders Forum on Sept. 30, reuniting former garrison commanders, command sergeants major, retired Marine joint base deputies, and command spouses. Following lunch at America’s Kitchen and an installation tour visiting the interim caisson village, participants gathered at Spates Hall for an open discussion. Current leadership consulted with the returning veterans on persistent base challenges, including aging utility infrastructure, histo
items.body:
**JOINT BASE MYER-HENDERSON HALL, Va. –**Decades of institutional memory, shared camaraderie, and dedicated service converged on Sept. 30 as Joint Base Myer-Henderson Hall hosted its inaugural Legacy Leaders Forum. The day brought together former garrison commanders, command sergeants major, Marine joint base deputies, chiefs of staff, executive officers, and command spouses to reconnect with the installation, chat with current staff, and trade insights on the unique realities of leading one of the nation’s most historic military communities.

The gathering kicked off over a lunch at America’s Kitchen, where the atmosphere felt more like a long-awaited family reunion than a leadership seminar. Several current garrison directors and chiefs dropped in to greet their former commanders and mentors, sharing laughs and catching up on both personal news and how operations have evolved since they last shared an office.

The roll call of returning leaders represented several generations of base leadership. Among those attending in person were Maj. Gen. (R) Kimberly Peeples, who served as garrison commander from 2018 to 2021; Command Sgt. Maj. (R) Carolyn Donaldson, garrison command sergeant major from 2016 to 2017; former Garrison Chief of Staff Carrie Mead; and former Executive Officer Tom Silvak. The Marine Corps side of the joint base partnership was represented by retired Marine LtCols Mark A. Paolicelli, Eric Kelly, and James Washburn, all of whom previously served as joint base deputies, with Washburn holding the distinct honor of serving as the installation’s very first joint base deputy.

Longtime garrison spouse leadership was also represented by Ms. Nancy Cook, whose husband Col. (R) Michael Cook commanded from 1991 to 1992, and Mrs. Helen Deibler, whose husband Col. (R) Scott Deibler led the garrison from 1992 to 1995. Even those unable to travel made sure to take part, with former garrison commander Col. (R) Thomas Allmon, who commanded from 2004-2007 and Marine LtCol John Dexter joining the group virtually.

Following lunch, the legacy leaders climbed aboard for a windshield tour across the installation to see what has changed and what has remained constant over the years. Along the way, the group made a brief stop at the Interim Stables for a quick walkthrough before heading over to Spates Hall to start the afternoon discussion.

Inside Spates Hall, current Garrison Commander Col. Keith Sandoval, Command Sgt. Maj. Kenyon Simmons, and Garrison Chief of Staff Tekeyiah Richardson led an honest, transparent conversation about the ongoing issues facing the joint base today. Many of the operational issues discussed were all too familiar to the legacy leaders in the room. The team laid out persistent hurdles including aging underground utilities across the installation, the rising cost to upkeep historic housing, and regional hiring and retention challenges across the competitive National Capital Region.

The team also shared some good news, including the $6.1M set aside for the exterior renovations to Old Post Chapel, the upcoming groundbreaking of the 200-bed barracks project starting in early FY27, and the recent announcement of the JBM-HH Army Community Service Team being named the 2026 Medium-Sized Garrison ACS of the Year.

Sandoval emphasized that yesterday’s gathering was just the beginning of a broader effort to tap into the wealth of experience sitting across the room and online.

"This forum is about recognizing that we stand on the shoulders of dedicated leaders who wrestled with many of these very same realities," Sandoval said. "Our hope is that this becomes a yearly event, and more importantly, the first step in putting together a permanent Legacy Leaders Council to provide our command team with seasoned insight, mentorship, and advice as we make decisions for the joint base."

For those who previously sat in the commander's chair, returning to the installation brought both nostalgia and an appreciation for the enduring mission of JBM-HH.

"Today was a powerful day,” Peeples said. “I’m grateful to the Joint Base team for inviting former leaders back to America’s Post to see the progress, share experiences, and reflect on the history and significance of this remarkable place. Most of all, I’m grateful for the Soldiers, Marines, civilians, families, leaders, and teammates who continue to serve this important Garrison mission with loyalty and selflessness. Itwas a true honor to be part of it.”

Simmons echoed the value of maintaining close bonds between today's garrison staff and those who paved the way.

"The institutional memory in this room represents decades of real-world problem-solving and caring for service members and their families," he added. "Spending time with the leaders who walked this ground before us helps put today's challenges in perspective. Their advice reinforces our commitment to our workforce and reminds us why this joint base community is so special."

As the afternoon wrapped up, participants lingered in the Freedom Lounge to share final stories, expressing broad enthusiasm for formalizing the advisory council and returning next year to keep the conversation going.

items.title: United We Sail: Sustaining the Fleet Since 1949
items.author: Molly Burgess
items.summary: The salt air leaves the same crust on your collar whether you are steering an oiler through the Korean Straits in 1950 or navigating an expeditionary sea base through the Arabian Gulf in 2026. Ship classes come and go, navigation bridges shift from paper charts to glowing touchscreens, but the core rhythm of the merchant mariner never changes - stand the watch, stay the course, and deliver the cargo.
items.body:
The salt air leaves the same crust on your collar whether you are steering an oiler through the Korean Straits in 1950 or navigating an expeditionary sea base through the Arabian Gulf in 2026. Ship classes come and go, navigation bridges shift from paper charts to glowing touchscreens, but the core rhythm of the merchant mariner never changes - stand the watch, stay the course, and deliver the cargo.

For 77 years, the heartbeat of Military Sealift Command has belonged to the Civil Service Mariners (CIVMARs), the seagoing professionals whose office is the open ocean and whose dedication underpins global national security.

“Seventy-seven year ago, Vice Adm. William M. Callaghan stood up the Military Sea Transportation Service at the Main Navy and Munitions building in Washington D.C.,” said Rear Adm. Benjamin Nicholson, Commander, Military Sealift Command. “Could anyone have imagined how the mission set for this command would grow and what a vital role we would one day play in our nation’s national security?”

October 1, 1949, marked the day of inception for Military Sea Transportation Service (MSTS), becoming the single managing agency for the Department of Defense’s ocean transportation needs, replacing what used to encompass four separate government agencies. MSTS would go on to be renamed Military Sealift Command during the Vietnam War.

To celebrate MSC turning another year older, the command held a cake cutting ceremony at MSC Headquarters onboard Naval Station Norfolk, Norfolk, Virginia, where the longest serving local CIVMAR, Chief Engineer Joseph Watts, and the newest MSC employee, James Caruthers, cut the first slice of cake in celebration of the command’s past sacrifices and today’s current workforce.

“Today we recognize and celebrate our CIVMARs, past and present, and the civilians and service members who have supported them in helping MSC deliver 77 years of maritime excellence,” said Nicholson.

Watts, who joined MSC Sept. 1, 1981, and is currently assigned to USNS Comfort (T-AH 20), said it’s the environment surrounding MSC that has contributed to his long career as a CIVMAR.

“MSC is a family organization and it’s what has kept me here for so long,” said Watts. “The mentoring that MSC has provided me and my family has been amazing.”

James Caruthers, a civilian at MSC who works as part of the IT Cybersecurity team, is the command’s newest employee having joined the team Sept. 21, 2026.

“Since being on board, I have had a lot of people welcome me to the team and help me with everything I need,” Caruthers said. “Being at MSC has truly been a breath of fresh air.”

For 77 years, CIVMARs aboard MSC vessels have served as the vital lifeline for the global warfighter. From transferring troops and armor during the Korean and Vietnam Wars to sustaining strategic deterrence throughout the Cold War, MSC has logistically driven nearly every major U.S. conflict. Today, MSC remains the steady force behind the front lines, keeping the joint force fueled, supplied, and positioned for victory.

“Thank you for what you do every single day and for the excellence you bring to this command and thank you to the families that support our teams who also greatly sacrifice,” Nicholson said. “Every one of you is part of our story and I look forward to creating many more memories with the Mariners, Sailors and Civilians of MSC.”

MSC exists to support the joint warfighter across the full spectrum of military operations, with a workforce that includes approximately 6,000 Civil Service Mariners and 1,500 contract mariners, supported by 1,500 shore staff and 3,500 active duty and reserve military personnel.

items.title: Space Force Sunsets 1970s-Era Missile Warning Satellite Constellation
items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: More than 50 years after the U.S. military launched its first Defense Support Program satellite, the Space Force has officially decommissioned the missile warning constellation as it prepares to start fielding its next-generation architecture. The post Space Force Sunsets 1970s-Era Missile Warning Satellite Constellation appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
More than 50 years after the U.S. military launched its first Defense Support Program satellite, the Space Force has officially decommissioned the missile warning constellation as it prepares to start fielding its next-generation architecture.

In a swan song of sorts, the last two remaining DSP spacecraft participated in a U.S. Space Command exercise in early September, helping the command demonstrate dynamic maneuvers across multiple orbits. Following the demonstration, the satellites were decommissioned into a supersynchronous—or graveyard—orbit, the Space Force’s Combat Forces Command said Oct. 1.

“These last two satellites were the culminating end to over a half-century of space-based early warning,” Mission Delta 4 Commander Col. Brandon Davenport said in a statement. “The DSP constellation ensured deterrence during the Cold War and protected our deployed warfighters from the Gulf War until their retirement last month.”

The first DSP satellite was launched in 1970 to geosynchronous orbit, providing key ballistic missile warning capabilities amid Cold War tensions between the U.S. and the Soviet Union. The goal was to discourage a first strike from the Soviets and help stabilize the relationship between the two nuclear-armed states. As the U.S. built out the constellation, it was used to detect theater missile launches in Iraq during the Operation Desert Storm in 1991. Its infrared sensors have also been used to detect natural disasters like forest fires and volcanic eruptions.

The constellation eventually grew to 23 satellites, the last of which launched in 2007. However, the service life of that final spacecraft was cut short in 2008 when a component failure caused it to drift to an unintended orbit. The Defense Department had originally set out to launch a 24th satellite, but ultimately canceled that plan. A full-sized DSP test article is on display at the National Museum of the United States Air Force in Dayton, Ohio.

DSP’s immediate successor, the Space-Based Infrared System, is on orbit today and consists of six satellites in GEO as well as four in a highly elliptical orbit. The Space Force is on the verge of launching the first of two Next-Generation Overhead Persistent Infrared satellites in the coming months. The spacecraft will augment the SBIRS constellation with improved, more sensitive sensors to detect dimmer threats.

Those two Next-Gen OPIR satellites, going to geosynchronous orbit, are part of the Space Force’s plan for a multiorbit missile warning architecture, which will include proliferated constellations in medium-Earth orbit and low-Earth orbit developed by Space Systems Command and the Space Development Agency, respectively. The service also had plans to fly two Next-Gen OPIR Polar satellites, but proposed canceling the program in its fiscal 2027 budget request. House and Senate lawmakers have supported maintaining the effort in drafts of defense spending and policy legislation, but its future will remain undecided until a final appropriations bill passes both chambers.

In its press release, Combat Forces Command noted that sunsetting the last two DSP satellites will allow operators in the 2nd Space Warning Squadron to shift their focus toward preparing for launch and initial testing of the first Next-Gen OPIR satellites.

“Retiring our legacy DSP system allows us to best posture for the future,” said Lt. Col. Ann Hughes, the squadron commander. “Our crews are always ready on each and every system they operate to ensure seamless [missile warning and tracking]. Onboarding future systems requires training for every scenario from unforeseen software issues to countering adversary aggression on orbit. We’re focused on providing a reliable, consistent, and seamless picture of missile threats regardless of the operational environment.”
